## The idea

Play the white notes from A to A and pay attention to the last step. G rises a
whole tone to A, so the arrival lacks the tight leading-tone motion heard from B
to C. Composers have often altered the upper part of the scale when they wanted
more pull or a smoother melodic route. Minor therefore behaves as a related
family of forms, not as one fixed row of notes.

*Natural minor* rotates the major-scale pattern so that it begins on degree 6.
*Harmonic minor* raises degree 7 in both directions, creating a leading tone.
*Melodic minor* raises degrees 6 and 7 on the ascent, then returns to natural
minor while descending. Treated as three rows of note names, the forms can look
like historical facts to memorise. Comparing their arrays reveals the purpose of
each edit: one creates a leading-tone approach to the tonic, while a second
removes the wide melodic gap on the way to that raised note.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 108
use_synth :piano

define :play_phrase do |notes|
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.35
    sleep 0.5
  end
end

natural = [57, 59, 60, 62, 64, 65, 67, 69]
harmonic = [57, 59, 60, 62, 64, 65, 68, 69]
melodic_up = [57, 59, 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 69]
melodic_down = natural.reverse

puts "harmonic changes: #{natural.zip(harmonic).select { |a, b| a != b }}"
puts "melodic changes: #{natural.zip(melodic_up).select { |a, b| a != b }}"

[natural, harmonic, melodic_up].each do |notes|
  play_phrase notes
  play_phrase notes.reverse
  sleep 1
end

play_phrase melodic_up + melodic_down.drop(1)

tune_degrees = [0, 2, 4, 3, 2, 5, 6, 7, 4, 3, 2, 1, 6, 7, 0]
[natural, harmonic, melodic_up].each do |scale_notes|
  play_phrase tune_degrees.map { |degree| scale_notes[degree] }
  sleep 1
end
```

The natural form keeps every adjacent step to one or two semitones. Harmonic
minor opens a three-semitone gap from F to G-sharp and supplies a semitone from
G-sharp to A. Melodic minor raises F to F-sharp during the ascent, replacing the
wide gap with smaller motions. Watch the printed diff while you listen for the
often-described increase in cadential pull; the code establishes the one- or
two-element change, while audition determines its character here.

## Change one thing

1. Lower harmonic minor's G-sharp to G in the final two notes only. The earlier
   altered notes remain, but the closing gesture loses its semitone approach to
   A. This separates the scale's general colour from its cadential use.
2. Use `:prophet` instead of `:piano` and set `release: 0.8`. The longer tails
   make F and G-sharp overlap, bringing the wide interval forward as a sound
   rather than a numerical difference.
3. Add 5 to every pitch in every array. The family moves from A to D while the
   differences between natural, harmonic, and melodic forms remain fixed.

## Why it works

Natural minor begins on degree 6 of its relative major, so rotating the major
formula yields `2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2`. Its seventh degree lies two semitones below
the tonic. Raise that degree and the final interval contracts to a semitone,
recreating the leading-tone pull that major supplies by default.

That harmonic solution creates a melodic complication. Natural degree 6 and
raised degree 7 are now three semitones apart. Harmony can make expressive use
of the gap, but a rising line often moves more fluently through smaller steps.
Melodic minor raises degree 6 too, making whole-tone steps through degrees 5, 6,
and 7. On the way down, degree 7 is no longer pressing toward a tonic above it,
so the natural form can return without frustrating that upward tendency.

The code keeps all three forms visible as data instead of hiding alterations in
the renderer. `zip` aligns corresponding positions, and `select` shows exactly
which ones changed. The tune can then consume any compatible eight-note array.
That separation lets you hear the scale choice against a fixed melodic design,
and it keeps the explanation close to the values responsible for the sound.

## Take it further

Write `minor_forms(root)` that returns `:natural`, `:harmonic`, `:melodic_up`,
and `:melodic_down` arrays in a hash. Generate them from step formulas rather
than copying note lists. Before listening, verify that natural and harmonic
minor differ at one index and that natural and melodic-up differ at two. Then
play a two-octave E-minor line, using the ascending form on the way up and the
descending form on the way back. The assertions protect the family resemblance;
the playback reveals what those small differences do.
